title: 第15章 探寺一第16章 探寺二
content_zh:
天还没亮透，杜五娘已经从后门出了府。
春杏提着灯笼走在前面，主仆二人都穿着粗布衣裳，脸上遮了帷帽，扮作寻常百姓家的女眷。
晨雾还没散，巷子里湿漉漉的青石板泛着幽光，像一面面破碎的镜子。
“五娘子，咱们真要去大相国寺？”春杏压低了声音，“老爷不是说了这几日不许府里的人出门。”
“你是我的人还是爹的人？”杜五娘冷冷地问了一句。
春杏不敢再说了。
昨夜那个梦像一根刺扎在杜五娘心口，怎么都拔不出来。
娘说的那些话，她不能当做没听见。
她要去找了尘方丈问个清楚，娘生前最信这个和尚，每月都要去烧香求福，他一定知道些什么。而且娘在梦里提到了了尘和尚的名字，说她将从爹那里偷听来的消息透露给他，这就是说娘和了尘之间有交易，不只是求符咒那么简单。
杜五娘攥紧了袖中的手。
大相国寺坐落在城东南，是京城数一数二的大寺，山门巍峨，香火鼎盛，天不亮就有信众在门外排队。
杜五娘到的时候，山门刚开不久，她没有从正门进，而是绕到侧面的小巷，找到一扇不起眼的角门。
这是柳氏从前带她来过的，了尘方丈给贵客留的私路，不用跟普通香客挤。
小门虚掩着，一推就开。
门后是一条青砖甬道，两侧是高高的院墙，墙头上爬满了枯藤。
深秋的晨风穿堂而过，呜呜咽咽的，好像有人在哭。
甬道尽头是一道月亮门，门后就是了尘的禅院。杜五娘让春杏在月亮门外等着，自己走了进去。禅院里静悄悄的，不见一个僧人。院子不大，中间种着一棵老槐树，树冠遮天蔽日，将整个院子罩在浓重的阴影里。树下摆着一只石盆，盆里养着几尾锦鲤，水面上浮着一层落叶，不知为何有些阴森。
禅房的门半敞着，杜五娘站在门外深吸了一口气，抬手敲门。
“方丈？”
没有人应答。她又敲了两下，门自己开了——不是被人拉开的，是风吹的。门轴发出吱呀一声长响，像是老人喉咙里挤出的叹息。

屋子里没有人，香炉里的香灰还是温的，砚台上的墨迹未干，显然不久前还有人在这里。
杜五娘环顾四周，目光落在那面墙上的观音画像上。
画不对，观音的眼睛是画上去的，但此刻那两只眼睛的位置是两个黑洞洞的窟窿。杜五娘走近了一些，伸手摸了摸，指尖触到的是冰冷的石壁。画像背后的墙应该有东西。她犹豫了一瞬，还是伸手揭开了画像。
画像后面是一道暗门，石门与墙壁严丝合缝，不仔细看根本发现不了。门上有只铜环，已经被人摸得铮亮，显然经常有人进出。杜五娘的心跳快了起来，她应该走的，一个闺阁女子不该在这种地方东翻西找，但她的手已经握住了铜环。
石门比她想象的要轻。门一开，一股阴冷潮湿的气息扑面而来，混杂着檀香、霉味和另一种说不清道不明的气味——腥的，甜的，像血。
石阶向下延伸，消失在黑暗中。杜五娘从袖中摸出一只火折子，催亮了火光。微弱的光只能照亮身前数步，石阶两侧的墙壁上刻满了诡异的符文，不是佛经，不是梵文，而是一种她从未见过的符号，弯弯曲曲的像蛇，又像扭曲的人形。
她数着石阶往下走，三十三级。尽头是一扇铁门，门上挂着一只铁锁，锁没有锁上，只是虚挂着。杜五娘取下铁锁，推开铁门，火光照亮了密室的全貌，她整个人僵在了门口。
密室不大，约莫两丈见方。正中央供奉着一座半人高的铜像，铜像面目狰狞，三头六臂，每一只手上都握着一样东西——刀剑、骷髅、人心。不是佛，不是菩萨，是邪神。
铜像前的供桌上摆着香炉、烛台，还有几只瓷碗。碗里盛着的东西在火折子的光里泛着暗红色，是血，已经干涸的血凝结在碗底，像一块块黑色的琥珀。供桌旁边有一只木架，上面整整齐齐地码着几十只黄布包裹的小包，和柳氏生前从大相国寺带回去的那些一模一样。
符咒，全是符咒。杜五娘走近了些，拿起其中一包拆开来看。黄布里面包着的不是符纸，而是一缕头发、一片指甲，还有一张写有生辰八字的纸条。她翻了翻那些纸条，上面的字有的是男人名字，有的是女人名字，有老有少，有达官贵人，也有平民百姓。每一个名字背后都是一个人，都是被了尘用符咒“照顾”过的人。
杜五娘的手开始发抖。就在这时，她听见身后传来一声轻微的响动——石门关上了。杜五娘猛地转身，火折子一晃差点熄灭。铁门还开着，但铁门外面那扇石门的背后站着一个披着袈裟的老僧——了尘。他不知什么时候跟下来的，无声无息，像一只在暗处潜伏的猫。
火光映在他脸上，一张平日里慈眉善目的脸，此刻看起来说不出的诡异。嘴角微微上扬，似笑非笑，眼底却没有任何温度。
content_en:
Before it gets bright, Du Wuniang has already left the house through the back door.
Chun Xing walked in front holding a lantern. Both the master and the servant were dressed in coarse cloth, with their faces covered with curtains and hats, pretending to be the female relatives of ordinary people.
The morning fog has not yet cleared, and the wet bluestone slabs in the alley are glowing like broken mirrors.
"Fifth Lady, do we really want to go to Daxiangguo Temple?" Chun Xing lowered her voice, "Didn't the master say that no one in the house is allowed to go out these days?"
"Are you mine or daddy's?" Du Wuniang asked coldly.
Chun Xing didn't dare to say anything anymore.
The dream last night was like a thorn in Du Wuniang's heart, and she couldn't pull it out no matter what.
She couldn't pretend she didn't hear what her mother said.
She was going to find Abbot Chen to find out. This was the monk whom my mother trusted the most during her lifetime. She would burn incense every month to pray for blessings. He must know something. Moreover, Mom mentioned the name of Monk Chen in her dream, saying that she would reveal to him the information she overheard from her father. This meant that there was a transaction between Mom and Chen, and it was not just as simple as asking for a charm.
Du Wuniang clenched her hands in her sleeves.
The Daxiangguo Temple is located in the southeast of the city. It is one of the largest temples in the capital.
When Du Wuniang arrived, the mountain gate had just opened. She did not enter through the main entrance, but went around to the side alley and found an inconspicuous corner door.
This was the place that Mrs. Liu had brought her here before, a private road left by Abbot Liaochen for distinguished guests, so they didn't have to squeeze in with ordinary pilgrims.
The small door is ajar and opens with a push.
Behind the door is a green brick corridor, with high courtyard walls on both sides, and the top of the wall is covered with dead vines.
The late autumn morning breeze passed through the hall, whimpering, as if someone was crying.
At the end of the corridor is a moon gate, and behind the gate is Ling Chen's Zen courtyard. Du Wuniang asked Chun Xing to wait outside the Moon Gate and walked in herself. The monastery was quiet, with not a single monk in sight. The yard is not big, and there is an old locust tree planted in the middle. The canopy of the tree blocks out the sky and the sun, casting a heavy shadow on the entire yard. There was a stone basin under the tree, with several koi carps in it. There was a layer of fallen leaves floating on the water, which looked a bit eerie for some reason.
The door of the Zen room was half open. Du Wuniang stood outside the door, took a deep breath, and raised her hand to knock on the door.
"Abbot?"
No one answered. She knocked twice more, and the door opened on its own—not by someone, but by the wind. The door hinge made a long creaking sound, like a sigh squeezed from an old man's throat.
There was no one in the room, the incense ashes in the incense burner were still warm, and the ink on the inkstone was still wet. It was obvious that someone had been here not long ago.
Du Wuniang looked around and her eyes fell on the portrait of Guanyin on the wall.
The painting is wrong. Guanyin's eyes were painted on, but at this moment, the positions of the two eyes are two dark holes. Du Wuniang came closer and reached out to touch. What she touched with her fingertips was the cold stone wall. There should be something on the wall behind the portrait. She hesitated for a moment, then reached out and uncovered the portrait.
Behind the portrait is a secret door. The stone door fits perfectly with the wall and cannot be found unless you look carefully. There is a copper ring on the door, which has been touched and shined. It is obvious that people come in and out often. Du Wuniang's heart beat faster. She should leave. A woman in a boudoir shouldn't be rummaging around in a place like this, but her hand was already holding the copper ring.
The stone door was lighter than she thought. As soon as the door opened, a cold, damp breath rushed in, mixed with sandalwood, musty smell and another unexplainable smell - fishy, ​​sweet, like blood.
The stone steps stretched downward and disappeared into the darkness. Du Wuniang took out a fire stick from her sleeve and lit the fire. The weak light could only illuminate a few steps in front of her. The walls on both sides of the stone steps were engraved with strange runes. They were not Buddhist scriptures or Sanskrit, but a symbol she had never seen before. They were curved like snakes and twisted human shapes.
She counted the stone steps going down, thirty-three. At the end is an iron door with an iron lock hanging on it.The lock was not locked, just hanging. Du Wuniang took off the iron lock and pushed open the iron door. The firelight illuminated the entire secret room, and she froze at the door.
The secret room is not big, about two feet square. In the center is a half-human-tall bronze statue with a ferocious face, three heads and six arms, and each hand holds something - a sword, a skull, and a human heart. Not a Buddha, not a Bodhisattva, but an evil god.
There are incense burners, candlesticks, and several porcelain bowls on the altar table in front of the bronze statue. The contents of the bowl glowed dark red in the light of the fire. It was blood. The dried blood condensed at the bottom of the bowl, like pieces of black amber. There is a wooden frame next to the offering table, with dozens of small bags wrapped in yellow cloth neatly stacked on it, which are exactly the same as the ones Liu brought back from Daxiangguo Temple during his lifetime.
Spells, all talismans. Du Wuniang walked closer, picked up one of the packages, opened it and looked at it. What was wrapped in the yellow cloth was not a talisman, but a lock of hair, a piece of fingernail, and a note with birth date written on it. She flipped through the notes. Some of the words on them were men's names, some were women's names, some were old and some were young, some were dignitaries, and some were ordinary people. Behind every name is a person, all of whom have been "taken care of" by Liao Chen using spells.
Du Wuniang's hands began to tremble. At this moment, she heard a slight sound behind her - the stone door was closed. Du Wuniang turned around suddenly, and the fire was almost extinguished in a flash. The iron gate was still open, but behind the stone door outside the iron gate stood an old monk wearing cassocks - Ling Chen. He didn't know when he followed her, silently, like a cat lurking in the dark.
The firelight reflected on his face, which was usually kind and kind, looked indescribably weird at the moment. The corners of his mouth were raised slightly, half-smiling, but there was no warmth in his eyes.
